## order-event.ts (core)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options d23313daea3a3f64
 */

/**
 * The order exists and has been costed.
 *
 * The discriminant is a literal type rather than a `string`, which is the whole
 * mechanism. `kind: string` would compile everywhere this does and narrow
 * nowhere, leaving every branch in every consumer looking at the union — an
 * ordinary interface with one field nobody can use.
 */
export interface OrderPlaced {
  readonly kind: "placed";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly total: number;
}

/**
 * It has left, and something outside now has custody of it.
 */
export interface OrderShipped {
  readonly kind: "shipped";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly carrier: string;
}

/**
 * It will not happen, and the reason is part of the record rather than a log
 * line.
 */
export interface OrderCancelled {
  readonly kind: "cancelled";
  readonly id: string;
  readonly reason: string;
}

/**
 * Exactly one of the shapes above — never two, and never a blend of them.
 *
 * The alternative most codebases reach for first is one interface with optional
 * fields: `{ kind: string; total?: number; carrier?: string }`. It costs
 * nothing to write and it makes every illegal combination representable —
 * shipped with a cancellation reason, placed with no total — so every reader
 * downstream has to decide what those mean, and each decides differently. The
 * union removes the question by removing the states.
 */
export type OrderEvent = OrderPlaced | OrderShipped | OrderCancelled;

/**
 * Every discriminant value, derived rather than restated.
 *
 * Written out by hand it would be a second list to keep in step with the first,
 * and the failure is silent: a member added to the union and forgotten here
 * leaves a handler map that no longer has to cover it.
 */
export type OrderEventKind = OrderEvent["kind"];

/**
 * Records that the order exists and has been costed.
 *
 * The declared return type is doing work. Without it the inferred `kind` widens
 * to `string`, and a value built here would not be assignable to the union — or
 * worse, in a wider context, would be assignable and then narrow to nothing.
 */
export function placed(id: string, total: number): OrderPlaced {
  return { kind: "placed", id, total };
}

/**
 * Records that it has left, and who has custody of it.
 */
export function shipped(id: string, carrier: string): OrderShipped {
  return { kind: "shipped", id, carrier };
}

/**
 * Records that it will not happen, and why.
 */
export function cancelled(id: string, reason: string): OrderCancelled {
  return { kind: "cancelled", id, reason };
}

/**
 * A discriminant nobody declared.
 *
 * Unreachable from typed code, and reachable from everywhere else: a value
 * parsed from JSON, a message from an older producer, a caller who is not using
 * TypeScript at all. The types stop at the module boundary and the data does
 * not, so the case that "cannot happen" gets a name and a value attached rather
 * than a crash somewhere further on.
 */
export class UnknownOrderEventError extends Error {
  readonly received: unknown;

  constructor(received: unknown) {
    super(`unhandled OrderEvent: ${JSON.stringify(received)}`);
    this.name = "UnknownOrderEventError";
    this.received = received;
  }
}

/**
 * One handler per case, keyed by the discriminant.
 *
 * `Extract` is what gives each handler the narrowed member rather than the
 * union, so a handler reading a field belonging to a different case does not
 * compile. Mapped over the discriminant rather than written out, so a member
 * added to the union adds a required key here — and every handler map in the
 * program stops compiling until it is covered.
 */
export type OrderEventHandlers<R> = {
  readonly [K in OrderEventKind]: (
    event: Extract<OrderEvent, { kind: K }>,
  ) => R;
};

/**
 * Applies the handler for whichever case arrived.
 *
 * Generic in the discriminant, which is what makes the body cast-free. Written
 * as `(event: OrderEvent)` instead, `handlers[event.kind]` is a union of all
 * three handler types, so its parameter is their intersection — `never`, since
 * the discriminants conflict — and the call has to be forced through with `as
 * never`. Keeping the key and the member related by a type parameter means the
 * compiler can see they match.
 *
 * The gain is smaller than it first looks, and worth stating exactly rather
 * than generously. A caller cannot tell the two versions apart: the handler
 * map's own type constrains every handler at the call site either way, and
 * swapping this body for the `as never` one breaks no assertion in this bundle
 * — which was checked, not assumed. What changes is inside. With the cast, that
 * the key used to find the handler matches the event handed to it is asserted
 * by whoever wrote the line, and `never` would have accepted any event at all;
 * here it is checked.
 */
export function match<R, K extends OrderEventKind>(
  event: Extract<OrderEvent, { kind: K }>,
  handlers: OrderEventHandlers<R>,
): R {
  const handler = handlers[event.kind];

  // Unreachable from typed code, for the reason `UnknownOrderEventError`
  // describes: a value from outside can carry a discriminant no handler has a
  // key for, and `handler` is then `undefined`. Without this the failure is a
  // `TypeError` about calling undefined, which names neither the value nor the
  // union it failed to match.
  if (handler === undefined) {
    throw new UnknownOrderEventError(event);
  }

  return handler(event);
}

/**
 * One answer per case.
 *
 * Nothing here asserts completeness, because nothing has to: the map's type
 * requires every key, so this function could not have been written with a case
 * missing. That is the difference from the `switch` form, where completeness
 * depends on each author remembering a default branch.
 */
export function summarise(event: OrderEvent): string {
  return match(event, {
    placed: (only) => `${only.id} placed (${String(only.total)})`,
    shipped: (only) => `${only.id} shipped (${only.carrier})`,
    cancelled: (only) => `${only.id} cancelled (${only.reason})`,
  });
}
```

## order-event-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern discriminated-union
 * @options d23313daea3a3f64
 */

/**
 * Using the union, and the mistakes it refuses.
 *
 * The refusals at the end are assertions rather than a demonstration: each
 * `@ts-expect-error` states that the line under it must *not* compile. The
 * guarantee this pattern exists for is that a case cannot be quietly left out,
 * and a guarantee nothing asserts is a hope — so it is pinned here, in a file
 * emitted whether or not the caller wanted tests.
 */

import { cancelled, match, placed, shipped } from "./order-event.js";
import type { OrderEvent, OrderEventKind, OrderPlaced } from "./order-event.js";

/**
 * A history, built through the constructors.
 *
 * The annotation is load-bearing rather than decorative. Each constructor
 * declares its return type, so `kind` stays a literal and these values belong
 * to the union; were those annotations dropped, `kind` would be inferred as
 * `string` and this array — which looks like the most ordinary line in the file
 * — would stop compiling.
 */
export const history: readonly OrderEvent[] = [
  placed("A-1", 2500),
  shipped("A-1", "royal-mail"),
  cancelled("A-1", "out-of-stock"),
];

/**
 * A second consumer, written the same way as the first.
 *
 * The point of the record form is what happens to this function when a fourth
 * member is added: it stops compiling, here, naming the key it is missing.
 * Nobody has to have anticipated that.
 */
export function notify(event: OrderEvent): string {
  return match(event, {
    placed: (placedEvent) =>
      `invoice ${placedEvent.id} for ${String(placedEvent.total)}`,
    shipped: (shippedEvent) =>
      `tracking for ${shippedEvent.id} via ${shippedEvent.carrier}`,
    cancelled: (cancelledEvent) =>
      `refund ${cancelledEvent.id}: ${cancelledEvent.reason}`,
  });
}

/**
 * Counting by case.
 *
 * A second place completeness is enforced structurally, and it works in either
 * dispatch style: `Record<OrderEventKind, number>` requires every key, so the
 * initialiser cannot omit a case and cannot invent one. Add a member to the
 * union and this stops compiling too.
 */
export function tally(
  events: readonly OrderEvent[],
): Record<OrderEventKind, number> {
  const counts: Record<OrderEventKind, number> = {
    placed: 0,
    shipped: 0,
    cancelled: 0,
  };

  for (const event of events) {
    counts[event.kind] += 1;
  }

  return counts;
}

/**
 * Folding a history into a state.
 *
 * The reason to model events this way rather than mutating a record: the state
 * is a function of the events, so it can be recomputed, and a state that was
 * never reachable through these transitions cannot be represented.
 */
export function outcome(
  events: readonly OrderEvent[],
): "open" | "shipped" | "cancelled" {
  return events.reduce<"open" | "shipped" | "cancelled">((state, event) => {
    if (event.kind === "shipped") return "shipped";
    if (event.kind === "cancelled") return "cancelled";

    return state;
  }, "open");
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * `@ts-expect-error` inverts the usual reading: it is satisfied by an error and
 * violated by silence. Each directive sits alone on its line with the reason
 * above it, because a directive only governs the line it begins on and a long
 * comment gets re-wrapped.
 *
 * Where the error is a property of an object, the directive sits inside the
 * object, on the line above that property. Above the whole statement it would
 * break for a long enough type name: the literal then wraps, the error is
 * reported against the property's own line, and the directive governs only the
 * `const` — so the assertion silently inverts into two errors, one for the
 * escaped mistake and one for a directive with nothing left to suppress. A
 * comment inside a literal also stops the formatter collapsing it, so the shape
 * does not depend on the name.
 */

export function refusesAnIncompleteDispatch(event: OrderEvent): string {
  // A handler map missing a case is not a valid map, so this cannot be written.
  // @ts-expect-error
  return match(event, {
    placed: (placedEvent) => placedEvent.id,
    shipped: (shippedEvent) => shippedEvent.id,
  });
}

export function refusesABlendedValue(): void {
  // "placed" carries a total and not a carrier. In one interface with optional
  // fields this would be an ordinary value, and every reader would have to
  // decide what it meant.
  const bad: OrderPlaced = {
    kind: "placed",
    id: "A-1",
    // @ts-expect-error
    carrier: "royal-mail",
  };

  void bad;
}

export function refusesTheWrongField(event: OrderEvent): void {
  if (event.kind === "placed") {
    // Narrowed to OrderPlaced, which has no carrier.
    // @ts-expect-error
    const bad: string = event.carrier;

    void bad;
  }
}

export function refusesAnUndeclaredKind(): void {
  // The set of cases is closed. A discriminant nobody declared is not a member
  // of the union, which is why the run-time check for one exists only for
  // values arriving from outside the type system.
  const bad: OrderEvent = {
    // @ts-expect-error
    kind: "refunded",
    id: "A-1",
    total: 2500,
  };

  void bad;
}
```
